danish.title: Sjette bog (1808–10) — Kapitel 19
paragraphs: Næste dag aflagde fyrst Andrej besøg i nogle huse, han ikke havde besøgt før, og deriblandt hos Rostoverne, med hvem han havde fornyet bekendtskabet ved ballet. Foruden de høflighedshensyn, der krævede besøget, ønskede han at se den originale, ivrige pige, der havde gjort et så behageligt indtryk på ham, i hendes eget hjem.

Natasja var en af de første til at møde ham. Hun var iført en mørkeblå hjemmekjole, hvori fyrst Andrej syntes, hun var endnu smukkere end i sin balkjole. Hun og hele Rostov-familien bød ham velkommen som en gammel ven, ligefrem og hjerteligt. Hele familien, som han førhen havde bedømt strengt, forekom ham nu at bestå af fortræffelige, ligefremme og venlige mennesker. Den gamle greves gæstfrihed og godmodighed, der i Petersborg slog én som en behagelig overraskelse, var af en art, så fyrst Andrej ikke kunne afslå at blive til middag. »Ja,« tænkte han, »de er prægtige mennesker, som naturligvis ikke aner, hvilken skat de besidder i Natasja; men de er venlige folk og udgør den bedst tænkelige ramme om denne slående poetiske, bedårende pige, der er fyldt med livslyst!«

I Natasja var fyrst Andrej sig bevidst om en mærkelig verden, fuldstændig fremmed for ham og sprængfyldt med glæder, han ikke kendte, en anden verden, som allerede i alléen på Otradnoje og ved vinduet den måneskinsnat havde begyndt at forstyrre ham. Nu forstyrrede denne verden ham ikke længere og var ham ikke længere fremmed; han selv havde trådt ind i den og fandt i den en ny nydelse.

Efter middagen gik Natasja på fyrst Andrejs opfordring hen til klaveret og begyndte at synge. Fyrst Andrej stod ved et vindue og talte med damerne og lyttede til hende. Midt i en sætning holdt han op med at tale og følte pludselig, at tårerne kvalte ham — noget han havde troet umuligt for ham. Han betragtede Natasja, mens hun sang, og noget nyt og glædeligt rørte sig i hans sjæl. Han følte sig lykkelig og samtidig bedrøvet. Han havde absolut intet at græde over, og dog var han parat til at græde. Over hvad? Sin tidligere kærlighed? Den lille fyrstinde? Sine skuffelser?... Sine fremtidshåb?... Ja og nej. Hovedårsagen var en pludselig, levende fornemmelse af den forfærdelige modsætning mellem noget uendeligt stort og grænseløst i ham og dette begrænsede og materielle noget, som han — og endda hun — var. Denne modsætning tyngede og dog opmuntrede ham, mens hun sang.

Så snart Natasja var færdig, gik hun hen til ham og spurgte, om han kunne lide hendes stemme. Hun spurgte det og blev derefter forvirret, idet hun følte, at hun ikke burde have spurgt. Han smilede, betragtede hende og sagde, at han kunne lide hendes sang, som han kunne lide alt, hvad hun foretog sig.

Fyrst Andrej forlod Rostovernes hus sent om aftenen. Han lagde sig af vane, men indså snart, at han ikke kunne sove. Han tændte sit lys og satte sig op i sengen, stod derpå op og lagde sig igen, ikke det mindste plaget af sin søvnløshed: hans sjæl var lige så frisk og glad, som var han trådt ud af et indelukket rum og ud i Guds egen friske luft. Det faldt ham ikke ind, at han var forelsket i Natasja; han tænkte ikke på hende, men forestillede sig hende blot for sit indre blik, og som følge deraf fremtrådte hele livet i et nyt lys. »Hvorfor stræber jeg, hvorfor slider jeg i denne snævre, begrænsede ramme, når livet, hele livet med alle dets glæder, ligger åbent for mig?« sagde han til sig selv. Og for første gang i meget lang tid begyndte han at lægge lykkelige planer for fremtiden. Han besluttede, at han måtte tage sig af sin søns opdragelse ved at finde en huslærer og sætte drengen i hans varetægt; derpå burde han tage sin afsked fra tjenesten og rejse til udlandet og se England, Schweiz og Italien. »Jeg må bruge min frihed, mens jeg føler så megen styrke og ungdom i mig,« sagde han til sig selv. »Pierre havde ret, da han sagde, at man må tro på muligheden af lykke for at blive lykkelig, og nu tror jeg på den. Lad de døde begrave deres døde, men mens man har livet, må man leve og være lykkelig!« tænkte han.

english.title: Book Six (1808 - 10) — Chapter 19
paragraphs: The next day Prince Andrew made calls at several houses he had not previously visited, including the Rostovs', with whom he had renewed his acquaintance at the ball. Apart from considerations of politeness that required the visit, he wanted to see that original, eager girl who had left such a pleasant impression on him — this time in her own home.

Natasha was one of the first to greet him. She was wearing a dark blue house dress in which Prince Andrew thought her even prettier than in her ball gown. She and the entire Rostov family welcomed him as an old friend — simply and warmly. The whole family, whom he had formerly judged harshly, now seemed to him to consist of excellent, straightforward, and kindly people. The old count's hospitality and good nature, which in Petersburg came as a particularly pleasant surprise, were such that Prince Andrew could not refuse to stay for dinner. "Yes," he thought, "they are wonderful people who of course have no idea what a treasure they possess in Natasha; but they are kind folk and make the best possible setting for this strikingly poetic, charming girl, so full of life!"

In Natasha, Prince Andrew sensed a strange world completely unlike his own, brimming with joys he had never known — a different world that had already begun to unsettle him in the Otradnoe avenue and at the window that moonlit night. Now this world no longer unsettled him and was no longer foreign; having entered it himself, he found in it a new kind of pleasure.

After dinner, at Prince Andrew's request, Natasha went to the clavichord and began to sing. Prince Andrew stood by a window talking to the ladies and listened to her. In the middle of a sentence he stopped speaking and suddenly felt tears rising in his throat — something he had thought impossible for him. He looked at Natasha as she sang, and something new and joyful stirred in his soul. He felt happy and at the same time sad. He had absolutely no reason to cry, yet he was on the verge of tears. About what? His former love? The little princess? His disillusionment? His hopes for the future? Yes and no. The main thing was a sudden, vivid awareness of the terrible contrast between something infinitely vast and boundless within him and the limited, material thing that he — and even she — actually was. This contrast weighed on him and yet lifted him while she sang.

As soon as Natasha finished, she went up to him and asked how he liked her voice. She asked this and then grew confused, feeling she shouldn't have asked. He smiled, looking at her, and said he liked her singing as he liked everything she did.

Prince Andrew left the Rostovs' late that evening. He went to bed from habit but soon realized he could not sleep. Having lit his candle he sat up in bed, then got up, then lay down again, not at all bothered by his sleeplessness: his soul was as fresh and joyful as if he had stepped out of a stuffy room into God's own open air. It didn't occur to him that he was falling in love with Natasha; he wasn't thinking about her directly, but only picturing her to himself — and as a result, all of life appeared in a new light. "Why do I struggle, why do I toil in this narrow, confined frame, when life — all life, with all its joys — lies open before me?" he said to himself. And for the first time in a very long while he began making happy plans for the future. He decided he must attend to his son's education by finding a tutor and entrusting the boy to his care, then he should retire from the service and go abroad — see England, Switzerland, and Italy. "I must make use of my freedom while I feel so much strength and youth in me," he told himself. "Pierre was right when he said one must believe in the possibility of happiness in order to be happy, and now I do believe in it. Let the dead bury their dead — while one has life, one must live and be happy!" he thought.
